difficultyReason: The paradox involves two interacting mechanisms: a medication that reduces average hospital stay lengths yet simultaneously increases total bed-days consumed. Resolution requires recognizing a compound demographic shift — the drug enables previously untreatable (and therefore unhospitalized) patients to now receive inpatient care, expanding the patient pool. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox and one that resolves only one horn.
stimulus: A new antibiotic reduces the average length of hospital stays for bacterial pneumonia patients by 30 percent compared to the previous standard treatment. Yet in the three years since the antibiotic was introduced nationwide, the total number of bed-days consumed annually by bacterial pneumonia patients has increased by 15 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiotic is significantly more expensive than the previous standard treatment, causing some hospitals to use it only selectively.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since the antibiotic's introduction, the number of patients hospitalized for bacterial pneumonia each year has grown by more than 60 percent, partly because the drug makes survival probable for previously unsurvivable cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibiotic requires intravenous administration for the first two days of treatment, after which patients may switch to oral medication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacterial pneumonia has become more prevalent in the general population over the same three-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hospitals that adopted the antibiotic earliest also implemented stricter discharge protocols that tend to extend average stays for all respiratory illnesses.

explanations.correct: If the hospitalized patient pool grew by over 60% while individual stay length fell 30%, total bed-days still rise substantially. This compound explanation accounts for both horns simultaneously: shorter stays per patient AND more total bed-days consumed.
explanations.A: Selective use might limit the antibiotic's reach, but this doesn't explain why total bed-days increased — it would more likely keep bed-days flat. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. A 60%+ increase in patient volume more than offsets a 30% reduction in stay length, explaining the rise in total bed-days despite shorter individual stays.
explanations.C: The administration route is irrelevant to the paradox; it doesn't explain why total bed-days increased.
explanations.D: Greater prevalence is consistent with the increase in bed-days, but it doesn't explain why bed-days rose despite shorter stays — it resolves only one horn and leaves the mechanism vague.
explanations.E: This deepens the paradox: if early adopters also extended stays, the average reduction of 30% should be harder to achieve, making the data internally inconsistent rather than resolved.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome (stricter sentencing) that correlates with rising crime rates. Resolution requires a reverse-causation plus confounding-variable mechanism: jurisdictions adopted stricter sentencing in response to already-rising crime, and the crime rate reflects a lag. Distractors include a 'deepens' trap and a definitional-mismatch near-miss.
stimulus: Over the past decade, jurisdictions that adopted mandatory minimum sentencing laws for drug offenses consistently show higher rates of drug-related crime than jurisdictions that did not adopt such laws. Yet criminologists agree that incarceration does reduce individual recidivism rates for those actually imprisoned.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws were disproportionately adopted by jurisdictions that already had the highest drug-crime rates at the time of adoption.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incarceration of low-level drug offenders frees up investigative resources, allowing police to detect more drug crimes than they could previously.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Criminologists who study recidivism typically focus on violent offenders rather than drug offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some jurisdictions with mandatory minimum sentencing have larger urban populations, where drug activity is inherently more concentrated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws are widely known to the public, which should deter first-time drug offenders more effectively than discretionary sentencing.

explanations.correct: If jurisdictions with mandatory minimums already had higher drug-crime rates before adopting the laws, the observed correlation reflects selection bias — high-crime jurisdictions chose the policy — rather than any causal effect of the laws. This reconciles higher post-adoption rates with the individual-level recidivism finding.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a classic selection/reverse-causation resolution: the laws were a response to high crime, not its cause. The correlation does not indicate failure of the policy on its own terms.
explanations.B: This deepens the paradox: if incarceration frees resources to detect more crime, reported crime should rise regardless of the policy's effectiveness, making it even harder to evaluate — but it doesn't resolve the inconsistency between aggregate and individual data.
explanations.C: A definitional mismatch trap: it weakens the recidivism evidence but doesn't explain why adopting jurisdictions have higher crime rates overall.
explanations.D: Urban-population size is a partial confounder, but it only addresses one horn — why crime is higher in those jurisdictions — without explaining why the aggregate rate didn't fall after the law's adoption.
explanations.E: This opposite-direction trap predicts the policy should work as a deterrent, which deepens rather than resolves the paradox by making the higher crime rates even more surprising.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves an environmental observation: a river's fish population declined sharply after a pollution cleanup. Resolution requires a compound mechanism — invasive species previously suppressed by the pollutant now thrive and outcompete native fish. Multiple distractors exploit plausible-sounding ecological mechanisms that resolve only one horn.
stimulus: After a decade-long program successfully reduced industrial pollutant levels in the Harrow River to near-pristine standards, researchers expected native fish populations to recover. Instead, annual fish-population surveys showed a 40 percent decline in native species over the five years following the cleanup's completion.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pollutants removed from the river had been acutely toxic to an invasive aquatic plant species that, now unchecked, has densely colonized the riverbed, destroying the spawning habitat native fish require.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced pollutant levels have attracted increased recreational fishing activity, raising the total annual catch of native species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native fish populations often take longer than five years to recover from chronic pollution exposure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some industrial facilities upstream were granted temporary exemptions and continued discharging low levels of the pollutant during the five-year survey period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cleanup program focused primarily on heavy metals, leaving organic chemical pollutants at levels still harmful to fish larvae.

explanations.correct: The pollutant, while harmful in general, also suppressed an invasive plant. Removing it unleashed the invasive species, which destroyed spawning habitat. This compound mechanism explains why cleaner water still produced a population decline — both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Correct. The hidden variable (invasive plant previously suppressed by the pollutant) explains why cleaner water paradoxically harmed native fish: the ecological balance shifted against them.
explanations.B: This deepens the paradox: increased fishing due to cleaner water could reduce populations, but it frames the decline as a consequence of success — this worsens rather than resolves the inconsistency with researcher expectations.
explanations.C: This resolves one horn only — it explains why populations haven't recovered — but doesn't explain the active 40% decline. Slow recovery is not the same as sharp decrease.
explanations.D: Continued low-level discharge might explain stagnant recovery, but not a 40% decline below pre-cleanup baselines. This resolves one horn only and doesn't account for the magnitude.
explanations.E: Residual organic pollutants could harm larvae, but this implies the cleanup was incomplete — it explains the failure to recover but not the sharp active decline, resolving one horn only.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves an economic finding: workers in a region earned higher wages after their primary employer downsized dramatically. The resolution requires identifying a compositional effect — low-wage workers were disproportionately laid off, raising the average wage of those remaining. Distractors include a 'deepens' trap and a misleading 'resolves partially' answer.
stimulus: When Veltran Manufacturing reduced its regional workforce by 45 percent over two years, economists predicted that average wages in the region would fall sharply due to oversupply of labor. Instead, regional wage surveys conducted immediately after the downsizing showed average wages had risen by 8 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The workers Veltran laid off were disproportionately entry-level and lower-skilled employees, whose departure raised the statistical average wage of the remaining regional workforce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Veltran Manufacturing offered generous severance packages to laid-off workers, temporarily sustaining consumer spending in the region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several technology firms announced plans to open facilities in the region within six months of the Veltran downsizing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Labor economists distinguish between median and average wages, and the surveys in question measured average wages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veltran retained its highest-paid engineers and managers while outsourcing production, which increased output per remaining employee.

explanations.correct: If the laid-off workers were predominantly lower-wage, their removal from the sample pool mathematically raises the average wage of those remaining — a classic compositional/measurement-artifact resolution. The 'average wage' figure reflects who is still employed, not any real wage increase for individuals.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a compositional effect: removing the lower end of a wage distribution raises the average. Economists' predictions assumed wages of remaining workers would fall, but the average was skewed by who left.
explanations.B: Severance sustaining consumer spending might slow economic contraction, but it doesn't explain why measured wages rose. This is irrelevant to the wage paradox.
explanations.C: Future tech-firm arrivals are consistent with eventual wage recovery, but they hadn't yet arrived — this resolves neither horn of the immediate post-downsizing data.
explanations.D: This identifies the measurement type (average vs. median) but doesn't explain why average wages rose — it merely restates a condition without providing the resolving mechanism.
explanations.E: Retaining high earners is part of the resolution mechanism but is less complete than A: it explains why high-wage workers remained but doesn't specify that lower-wage workers left in large numbers, which is the critical compositional driver.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a technology outcome: a software security patch reduced the rate of successful intrusions, yet total data breaches at patched organizations increased. Resolution requires a two-part mechanism: the patch redirected attackers toward a different, unpatched vulnerability class, and the newly exposed attack vector was more damaging. Distractors include a 'deepens' option and a 'one horn only' near-miss.
stimulus: A widely deployed cybersecurity patch successfully reduced successful network intrusions via malware injection by 55 percent at organizations that installed it. Yet in the year following the patch's deployment, those same organizations reported 30 percent more total data breaches than they had in the prior year.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The patch contained a configuration error that inadvertently disabled logging features, preventing organizations from detecting breaches in real time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attackers who were blocked by the patch shifted their efforts toward phishing campaigns targeting employee credentials, a vector the patch did not address, and phishing-based breaches increased fivefold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cybersecurity budgets at patched organizations increased substantially in the year following deployment, enabling more thorough breach audits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patch was most rapidly adopted by large organizations that handle greater volumes of sensitive data, making them more attractive targets overall.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The definition of 'data breach' used by regulators was expanded during the year in question to include previously unreported incident types.

explanations.correct: If attackers redirected efforts to phishing — an unaddressed vector — after the patch blocked malware injection, then malware intrusions fell while a different breach type surged, explaining both the reduction in intrusions and the net increase in total breaches. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Disabled logging would cause under-detection of breaches, not more breaches — and if anything would make reported breaches fall, which deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacker substitution to a new unpatched vector (phishing) explains why closing one vulnerability led to a net increase in breaches — the patch was effective at what it targeted, but displaced rather than eliminated attacks.
explanations.C: Better auditing could explain discovering more breaches, which is a partial resolution, but this is a 'resolves one horn only' trap — it doesn't explain why actual breaches increased, only why more were detected.
explanations.D: Large organizations being more attractive targets could explain higher breach rates at adopters, but it deepens the paradox by implying that the very act of patching increased targeting — without resolving the inconsistency.
explanations.E: An expanded regulatory definition is a definitional-mismatch resolution candidate, but it resolves only the reporting increase without explaining the actual breach data, and it doesn't account for the simultaneous drop in malware intrusions.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a historical pattern: literacy rates in a colony rose sharply during a period when the colonial government actively banned local-language education. The compound resolution involves a hidden variable: missionary organizations operating outside government control expanded vernacular literacy programs precisely in response to the ban. Distractors include a temporal mismatch and a deepens-the-paradox option.
stimulus: Between 1880 and 1900, the colonial administration of Northaven Province banned instruction in indigenous languages at all government-funded schools, mandating that all education occur exclusively in the colonial language. Yet census records show that literacy in indigenous languages among Northaven's adult population increased by 22 percent during this same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many adult residents of Northaven Province had already learned to read in the colonial language before 1880, which made learning to read in indigenous languages easier for them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The colonial administration's ban applied only to government-funded schools, while independent missionary societies, which operated outside government funding, dramatically expanded indigenous-language literacy programs after 1880 in direct response to the ban.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Literacy in the colonial language also increased during the same period, suggesting that overall educational attainment rose in Northaven Province between 1880 and 1900.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Census officials in 1900 used a broader definition of 'literacy' than their 1880 counterparts, counting partial reading ability as full literacy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The colonial government increased funding to government schools between 1880 and 1900, raising enrollment and improving educational outcomes in the colonial language.

explanations.correct: The ban applied only to government-funded schools. Missionary organizations — operating outside that funding — expanded indigenous-language programs in response to the ban, creating an alternative channel for literacy growth. This resolves both horns: the ban was real and enforced in its domain, yet literacy still rose through an independent, unregulated sector.
explanations.A: Transfer-of-literacy skills might facilitate learning a second script, but this is speculative and doesn't explain the institutional mechanism by which indigenous literacy rose despite the ban. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. The scope restriction (government-funded only) combined with the missionary expansion is a compound mechanism resolving both horns: the ban was effective within its scope, but the scope was limited, and other actors filled the gap.
explanations.C: Rising colonial-language literacy deepens rather than resolves the paradox — if colonial-language education was displacing indigenous education, we'd expect indigenous literacy to fall, not rise.
explanations.D: A definitional mismatch trap: an expanded census definition could inflate reported literacy, but it addresses only the measurement and doesn't explain the real-world educational dynamic. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Increased colonial-school funding and enrollment deepens the paradox: if more children entered colonial-language-only schools, indigenous-language literacy should have been further suppressed, making the 22% increase even harder to explain.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a linguistic finding: speakers of a language with grammatically obligatory evidential markers (words indicating how a speaker knows something) perform worse on source-monitoring memory tests than speakers of languages without such markers. Resolution requires recognizing that habitual outsourcing of source-tracking to grammar reduces the development of independent memory-based source monitoring. Distractors include a circular resolution and a deepens option.
stimulus: Languages that grammatically require speakers to mark whether their knowledge is firsthand, reported, or inferred — a feature linguists call evidentiality — are often assumed to sharpen speakers' attention to the source of their information. Yet controlled experiments consistently show that native speakers of obligatory-evidential languages perform significantly worse on laboratory source-monitoring memory tasks than speakers of languages without this feature.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speakers of obligatory-evidential languages rely on grammatical markers at the time of speaking to signal source information, which reduces the need to independently encode source details in memory during comprehension.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laboratory source-monitoring tasks were originally developed and normed using speakers of non-evidential languages, introducing a potential cultural bias in task design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidential markers in many languages are acquired early in childhood, suggesting they are deeply embedded in native speakers' cognitive processing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speakers of obligatory-evidential languages are more likely to correctly identify information as 'reported' versus 'inferred' in their daily communication than speakers of non-evidential languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The evidential languages studied are spoken primarily in regions with oral rather than literate traditions, which may affect memory strategies independently of grammatical structure.

explanations.correct: If grammatical markers handle source-signaling at the moment of speaking, speakers are not required to store source information deeply in memory — the grammar does the work. Consequently, independent memory-based source monitoring is less practiced and less developed, explaining the worse laboratory performance. Both horns are resolved.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a reverse-causation/cognitive-offloading mechanism: grammar's efficiency as a signaling system actually atrophies the independent memory capacity it was assumed to enhance.
explanations.B: Cultural bias in task design is a plausible methodological critique, but it resolves only the measurement horn — it doesn't explain why the effect is consistent across multiple controlled experiments or why evidential speakers perform worse rather than differently.
explanations.C: Early acquisition of evidential markers deepens rather than resolves the paradox: if the feature is deeply embedded cognitively, speakers should be even more attuned to source information, making the poor performance more surprising.
explanations.D: Better real-world source labeling in communication is consistent with evidentiality's function, but it resolves only one horn — it doesn't explain why this advantage doesn't transfer to memory tasks. This is a 'resolves one horn only' trap.
explanations.E: Oral tradition affecting memory strategies is a confounding-variable candidate, but it doesn't directly address the evidentiality mechanism and leaves the specific grammatical-feature paradox unexplained. Resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves a policy outcome: a city's ban on single-use plastic bags reduced plastic-bag litter but increased total plastic waste tonnage. Resolution requires a compound mechanism: consumers switched to reusable bags that require far more plastic per unit to manufacture, and the replacement rate was high enough that lifecycle plastic use increased. Distractors include a 'deepens' option and a partial-resolution near-miss.
stimulus: After Clearwater City banned single-use plastic bags at retail checkouts, surveys confirmed a 70 percent reduction in plastic-bag litter in the city's parks and waterways. Yet municipal solid-waste data showed that total plastic waste tonnage collected in Clearwater increased by 12 percent in the two years following the ban.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reusable bags that consumers purchased in response to the ban are made primarily of polypropylene, requiring roughly 40 times more plastic by weight per bag than single-use bags, and the majority of consumers replaced their reusable bags within 18 months rather than using them long-term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ban prompted Clearwater retailers to increase their use of plastic clamshell packaging for produce, which had previously been sold in bags that were exempt from the ban.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Municipal solid-waste collection in Clearwater expanded its coverage area in the same two-year period, annexing several suburban districts that had previously handled their own waste.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clearwater residents who remembered to bring reusable bags used them consistently, while residents who forgot brought reusable bags less often over time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 70 percent litter reduction was measured by visual survey, which may undercount small plastic fragments that make up a significant portion of plastic pollution.

explanations.correct: Reusable bags require 40x more plastic per unit, and consumers discarded them within 18 months — well before the lifecycle offset point. This compound mechanism explains both horns: litter fell (fewer lightweight bags escaping into the environment) while total plastic tonnage rose (heavier replacement bags accumulating in solid waste at high turnover rates).
explanations.A: Correct. The high per-unit plastic weight of reusable bags combined with rapid replacement creates a net plastic-tonnage increase, while the physical properties of single-use bags (light, wind-borne) explain the independent litter reduction. Both horns resolved.
explanations.B: Increased clamshell packaging is a partial resolution — it could explain some of the tonnage increase — but it doesn't account for the specific mechanism tied to the bag ban and doesn't resolve both horns together. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Expanded waste-collection coverage (annexing suburbs) would inflate reported tonnage regardless of the ban's effect. This is a measurement-artifact resolution, but it resolves only the tonnage horn and doesn't address the litter data. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Inconsistent reusable-bag usage describes consumer behavior but doesn't explain the tonnage increase — it would more likely suggest lower reusable-bag purchases, not higher plastic waste. Irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.E: Undercounting litter fragments addresses measurement validity in the litter survey, potentially weakening one horn, but it doesn't resolve why total plastic tonnage increased. Resolves one horn only and weakens rather than resolves.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves an arts/economics observation: auction prices for works by living artists rose sharply during a period when those artists' critical reputations, as measured by museum acquisitions and scholarly citations, declined. The compound resolution involves market segmentation: a new class of speculative collectors, uncorrelated with critical assessment, entered the market and drove prices up through demand that operated independently of institutional prestige.
stimulus: During the 1990s, average auction prices for works by living contemporary artists rose by over 200 percent in real terms. Over the same decade, the number of works by living contemporary artists acquired by major public museums fell by 35 percent, and scholarly citations of these artists in peer-reviewed art-history journals declined sharply.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Museum acquisition budgets were sharply reduced during the 1990s due to government arts-funding cuts, preventing museums from purchasing works regardless of their critical standing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Art-history scholarship in the 1990s shifted its focus toward historical periods and deceased artists, reducing citations of living artists across the board independently of those artists' commercial trajectories.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the 1990s, a large cohort of high-net-worth investors entered the contemporary art market treating works as financial assets, bidding prices up through speculative demand that was largely independent of institutional critical assessment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The auction houses that reported rising prices in the 1990s represented only the top tier of the contemporary art market, excluding mid-career and emerging artists whose prices remained flat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some major museums shifted from outright acquisition to long-term loan agreements, which would not appear in acquisition statistics but still reflected institutional engagement with living artists.

explanations.correct: A new class of speculative investors valuing art as a financial instrument drove auction prices independently of critical or institutional evaluation. This resolves both horns simultaneously: prices rose because of market demand from a new buyer segment, while critical and institutional indicators fell because scholarly and curatorial taste was moving in a different direction — the two metrics were measuring different things driven by different actors.
explanations.A: Budget cuts explain reduced museum acquisitions (one horn), but don't explain why auction prices rose. This is a resolves-one-horn-only trap.
explanations.B: A shift in scholarly focus explains declining citations (one horn) but doesn't explain the price surge. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Correct. Speculative investors constitute a new, independent demand driver for prices that operates outside the critical-prestige system measured by museum acquisitions and citations. Both horns are resolved by identifying the market segmentation.
explanations.D: A sampling artifact (top-tier auction data) could challenge the price-rise finding, but it resolves neither horn and introduces doubt about the stimulus's factual basis rather than explaining the discrepancy. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Long-term loans partially address the museum-acquisition horn by suggesting institutional engagement didn't fall as much as the data indicate, but it doesn't explain the price surge and resolves only one horn incompletely.

difficultyReason: The paradox involves an ethics/policy finding: a country that implemented a comprehensive national ethics code for public officials saw an increase in the number of prosecuted corruption cases in the years following implementation. Resolution requires recognizing a compound mechanism: the code created enforceable legal standards and independent oversight bodies where none existed, increasing detection and prosecution capacity rather than indicating more corruption. Distractors include a deepens option and a temporal-scope trap.
stimulus: Rendovia enacted a sweeping national ethics code for public officials in 2005, establishing mandatory disclosure requirements, an independent oversight commission, and criminal penalties for violations. Yet in the five years following the code's enactment, the number of public officials prosecuted for corruption in Rendovia increased by nearly 80 percent compared to the five years prior.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before 2005, Rendovia had no independent oversight body with subpoena power, and most corrupt acts by public officials were never investigated, let alone prosecuted; the new commission's authority and investigative resources substantially increased the detection and prosecution of conduct that had previously gone undetected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ethics code was drafted with input from international anti-corruption organizations, whose best-practice recommendations are widely regarded as effective in the long term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several high-profile corruption scandals involving senior officials were exposed by investigative journalists in 2006 and 2007, drawing public attention to corruption issues.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public officials in Rendovia were initially uncertain about the scope of the new disclosure requirements and may have inadvertently failed to comply, resulting in technical violations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rendovia's economy grew substantially between 2005 and 2010, increasing the total funds available to public officials and thereby raising the monetary stakes — and temptations — associated with public positions.

explanations.correct: The 80% increase in prosecutions reflects improved detection capacity — an independent commission with subpoena power investigating previously invisible conduct — rather than a genuine increase in corrupt behavior. This resolves both horns: the ethics code is consistent with anti-corruption goals because it exposed pre-existing corruption, and the rise in prosecutions is a success indicator, not a failure.
explanations.A: Correct. The prior absence of effective investigative infrastructure meant corruption was underprosecuted; the new commission's capacity explains the prosecution surge as a detection artifact, not an increase in actual corruption. Both horns resolved.
explanations.B: International best-practice credentials are irrelevant to the prosecution data — this doesn't explain why prosecutions rose after implementation. Irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Journalist-driven scandals might explain a few high-profile cases, but they don't account for an 80% systemic increase across all prosecutions, and they don't explain the mechanism by which the ethics code coexists with rising prosecutions. Resolves one horn only partially.
explanations.D: Technical violations from compliance confusion could contribute to some prosecutions, but this would suggest the code was poorly designed — a 'deepens the paradox' option implying the code itself generated the corruption it was meant to prevent.
explanations.E: Economic growth raising temptation is a reverse-causation trap: it implies corruption actually did increase, deepening rather than resolving the paradox by suggesting the ethics code failed to prevent corruption that genuinely worsened.
